I am not sure what subject you are giving on, so I’m going to keep it general:

1. Usually, people don't care about the introduction - if you are the first to present, then you'll have to go through it all... if you are like the 7th person for the same instructors, then you better keep it brief.

2. Talk about results for the most part - highlight them as how you have obtained good information, while ascertaining the scientific process was pretty good.

3. Keep conclusions brief (about 3-6 points) and then open the floor for questions.

4. Some professors will ask questions on the methodologies - you can guess they did not understand much, so you can answer them easily, confound them if you don't know well. Don't go too far though and get caught yourself.

5. Typical ones will ask you about interpretations of the results, how it will help, and might ask you what you could have done and could not have - in this case - if it was a cheap/easy experiment suggestion, tell why that data would not fit in your thesis. If it was a costly suggestion, say these were initial results and it can be probed further based on funding and resources. Most times they'll suggest something that starts discussions amongst themselves (the instructors), just keep nodding and smiling.

6. The insightful ones will challenge your premise and what could be the implications of your work. Answer the first part to the best of your knowledge while the second part sparingly, leaving it open-ended.

7. It's okay to say "I don't know" for 2 out of 10 questions but only if it is something you did not perform.

For example: you cannot say "I don't know" when the question is, "Why did you perform this and this experiment when you could have better quality of results using this experiment?"

You can say "I don't know" when they ask knowledge-based questions like "what is the melting point of that one random chemical you used in just one time and is not too relevant in your study as your experiments never take it to those temperatures." Such questions are better avoided - as it might open the floor for more knowledge-based questions.

8. Presentations are made to push you to your sweating point and to make you say "I don't know" at least a few times. Don't get too cocky nor look too foolish - pick and choose those "I don't knows" if possible, better if you can predict the next question based on your answer - sometimes they are designed to trap you.

9. Know the basics - 80% of your questions will be on the basics. There's no point in explaining your new algorithm when you don't know what the If-then code exactly does in your program.

10. When your advisor steps in to defend you, better let them answer. But make sure you are talking for at least 60% of the time for a good grade - else it'll seem like the advisor is answering all the questions. If you've passed that, let the advisor take the question - stay out of trouble, unless asked to specifically.
